summary: The six articles of faith (arkan al-iman) are the foundational beliefs every Muslim must hold: belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and divine decree. They are established by the Hadith of Jibril.
content:
The six articles of faith (arkan al-iman) define the essential content of Islamic belief. They were articulated by the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in response to the Angel Jibril, who came in human form and asked: 'Tell me about iman.' The Prophet replied: 'Iman is to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and to believe in divine decree — both the good and the seemingly bad of it.' Jibril said: 'You have spoken the truth' (Muslim 8).

This hadith — the Hadith of Jibril — is the primary textual source for understanding iman, islam, and ihsan as three distinct but interrelated dimensions of the religion.

## The Six Articles

### 1. Belief in Allah (al-Iman billah)
The first and most foundational article: affirming that Allah alone is the one true God, affirming His tawhid (oneness) in lordship, worship, and names and attributes. This encompasses belief in His existence, His perfect attributes, His absolute uniqueness, and the obligation to worship Him alone. See the article on Tawhid for the full treatment.

### 2. Belief in the Angels (al-Iman bil-Mala'ikah)
Angels are created beings made of light, created before humanity, who have no free will in disobeying Allah — they do exactly what they are commanded. They carry out divine decrees: Jibril brought revelation, Israfil will blow the Trumpet, Mika'il governs rain and provision, Azra'il (or Malak al-Mawt) takes souls, Munkar and Nakir question in the grave, Ridwan guards Jannah, Malik guards Jahannam, and the Kiraman Katibin record deeds. Belief in all angels, known and unknown, is obligatory.

### 3. Belief in the Revealed Books (al-Iman bil-Kutub)
Allah sent books to His prophets: the Suhuf (scrolls) to Ibrahim and Musa (in their original form), the Tawrah (Torah) to Musa, the Zabur (Psalms) to Dawud, the Injil (Gospel) to Isa, and the Quran to Muhammad (peace be upon them all). The Quran is the final, preserved, and authoritative revelation. Previous scriptures are honoured but acknowledged to have been altered over time and superseded. The Quran says: 'Indeed, it is We who sent down the Remembrance, and indeed We will guard it' (15:9).

### 4. Belief in the Messengers (al-Iman bil-Anbiya wal-Rusul)
Allah sent prophets to every nation with the message to worship Him alone. Muslims believe in all of them — denying even one is a nullifier of faith. The Quran mentions twenty-five by name; many others are not named. Muhammad (peace be upon him) is the final prophet and messenger, after whom there is no prophethood. See the article on Risalah for the full treatment.

### 5. Belief in the Last Day (al-Iman bil-Yawm al-Akhir)
This encompasses everything after death: the questioning in the grave, the Day of Resurrection, the gathering, the reckoning, the weighing of deeds, Jannah, and Jahannam. The believer's awareness of accountability on that Day shapes every action in this life. 'And the Day when He will gather you for the Day of Assembly — that is the Day of Deprivation (for the wrongdoers)' (64:9). See the article on al-Akhirah for the full treatment.

### 6. Belief in Divine Decree (al-Iman bil-Qadar)
Allah has perfect knowledge of all things, has written everything in al-Lawh al-Mahfuz (the Preserved Tablet), has willed all things, and has created all things. Nothing occurs outside His knowledge and will. This belief brings peace in hardship and gratitude in ease. See the article on Qadar for the full treatment.

## Iman: Definition and Nature

Ahl us-Sunnah define iman as belief in the heart (tasdiq), declaration with the tongue (iqrar), and action with the limbs (amal). It increases with obedience and decreases with disobedience — a position held against the Murji'ah, who excluded actions from iman, and against the Khawarij, who declared sinful Muslims disbelievers.

The Quran says: 'The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, it increases them in faith, and they rely upon their Lord' (8:2-4). This verse connects iman to both inner states and outward conduct.

## Islam, Iman, and Ihsan

The Hadith of Jibril distinguishes three levels:
- **Islam** — the five outward pillars
- **Iman** — the six inward beliefs
- **Ihsan** — worshipping Allah as though you see Him

These are not separate religions but three dimensions of the same faith, each deepening the next. A Muslim who perfects all three has reached the highest level of commitment to the religion.
evidence_quran: Surah al-Baqarah 2:177 — 'Righteousness is... to believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets'
Surah al-Baqarah 2:285 — 'The Messenger has believed in what was revealed to him from his Lord, and the believers; all of them have believed in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers'
Surah al-Hijr 15:9 — 'Indeed, it is We who sent down the Remembrance, and indeed We will guard it'
Surah al-Anfal 8:2-4 — 'The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble'
Surah at-Taghabun 64:9 — 'And the Day when He will gather you for the Day of Assembly'
evidence_hadith: Muslim 8 — Hadith of Jibril: the foundational hadith defining iman, islam, and ihsan
Bukhari 8 — 'Islam is built upon five' (pillars of islam, complementary to articles of iman)
Bukhari 9, Muslim 35 — Iman has seventy-odd branches, the highest is 'La ilaha illallah'
scholar_positions: The definition of iman as belief + declaration + action is the Athari and Hanbali position, affirmed by Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim. Ash'ari scholars define iman primarily as tasdiq (affirmation of the heart) and hold that actions are conditions of completeness rather than constitutive elements; this is an intra-Sunni scholarly difference. The Maturidi position is similar to the Ash'ari. Neither position is deviant; both are part of Ahl us-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah.
sources: al-Nawawi, Sharh Muslim (commentary on Hadith of Jibril, vol. 1)
Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali, Jami' al-'Ulum wal-Hikam (commentary on Hadith of Jibril)
Ibn al-Qayyim, al-Fawa'id (chapters on iman and its levels)
